youtube.title: Ceuta and Melilla: Why the EU's Only Land Borders in Africa Belong to Spain
youtube.description:
Ceuta and Melilla are two Spanish cities on the coast of Africa, surrounded by Morocco on land. Their fences are the European Union's only land borders on the African continent, and the Ceuta and Melilla history behind them reaches back to a Portuguese fleet in 1415. How did a treaty signed in Lisbon and the range of a single cannon shot leave Spain holding them, and what is Morocco's claim?

This video follows the map in the order it was drawn: the conquests, the treaty lines, Morocco's independence in 1956, the EU fences of the 1990s, and the border crises from 2018 to 2025. It sets out Morocco's claim and Spain's case in their own terms, then three roads that could change the map, from trade gates to the NATO question to the Gibraltar deal.

{CHAPTERS}

youtube.comment: Should a treaty from the 1600s still decide who rules a city today? 👇

sources.claim: Ceuta and Melilla are the EU's only land borders on the African continent
sources.source: European Parliament Research Service, briefing on EU external borders, 2021; Frontex, Western Mediterranean route profile

sources.claim: Ceuta's land border fence runs about 8 km, Melilla's about 12 km, about 20 km in all
sources.source: Spanish Ministry of the Interior, border perimeter figures, as reported by El País, 2020

sources.claim: About 170,000 people live in the two cities: Ceuta about 83,000, Melilla about 85,000
sources.source: INE (Spain's statistics institute), municipal register, 1 January 2023

sources.claim: Ceuta covers about 19 square kilometres, Melilla about 12 square kilometres
sources.source: INE, municipal surface areas; Ciudad Autónoma de Ceuta and Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla official data

sources.claim: The Strait of Gibraltar is about 14 km wide at its narrowest
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Strait of Gibraltar'

sources.claim: Ferries from Algeciras reach Ceuta in about an hour
sources.source: Baleària and FRS published timetables, 2025

sources.claim: Melilla lies about 225 km east of Ceuta, as the crow flies
sources.source: Great-circle distance between city coordinates (35.89N 5.32W and 35.29N 2.94W)

sources.claim: Spain also holds two tiny island groups, the Chafarinas Islands and the Alhucemas islands, and one rock joined to the mainland by sand, the Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera, whose land border with Morocco is about 85 metres
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Plazas de soberanía'; Peter Gold, 'Europe or Africa?', Liverpool University Press, 2000

sources.claim: Ceuta and Melilla are part of Spain and the EU but outside the EU customs territory
sources.source: Act of Accession of Spain and Portugal, 1985, Protocol No 2 concerning the Canary Islands and Ceuta and Melilla

sources.claim: El Tarajal is Ceuta's main border crossing, facing the Moroccan town of Fnideq
sources.source: Spanish Ministry of the Interior, list of authorised border crossing points; position measured on map

sources.claim: When Spain signed up to Schengen in 1991, residents of the Moroccan provinces of Tetouan and Nador could enter Ceuta and Melilla for the day without a Schengen visa, but not travel on to mainland Spain
sources.source: Agreement on the Accession of Spain to the Schengen Convention, Final Act, Declaration on Ceuta and Melilla, 25 June 1991

sources.claim: Schengen border checks were lifted for Spain on 26 March 1995
sources.source: Convention implementing the Schengen Agreement, put into effect 26 March 1995 for seven states including Spain; European Commission, Schengen area history

sources.claim: Melilla's triple fence was raised to about 10 metres on its most crossed stretches from 2019
sources.source: Spanish Ministry of the Interior announcement, 2019; works reported by El País, 2020

sources.claim: GDP per person in 2023: Spain about $33,500, Morocco about $3,700, about nine times as much
sources.source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, GDP per capita (current US$), 2023, rounded

sources.claim: A Portuguese fleet captured Ceuta in August 1415
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ceuta'

sources.claim: A Spanish force took Melilla in 1497, when it was largely abandoned, 82 years after Portugal took Ceuta in 1415
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Melilla' and 'Ceuta'

sources.claim: Spain and Portugal were under one king from 1580; Portugal broke away in 1640 and Ceuta stayed with Spain
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ceuta'; Peter Gold, 'Europe or Africa?', 2000

sources.claim: The Treaty of Lisbon of 1668 recognised Ceuta as Spanish
sources.source: Treaty of Lisbon, 13 February 1668; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ceuta'

sources.claim: Moroccan forces besieged Ceuta for 33 years, from 1694 to 1727
sources.source: Peter Gold, 'Europe or Africa?', 2000; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ceuta'

sources.claim: An 1859 treaty set Melilla's border at the range of a Spanish cannon; the shot was fired in 1862
sources.source: Convention of Tetouan, 24 August 1859; Peter Gold, 'Europe or Africa?', 2000

sources.claim: After the war of 1859 and 1860, the Treaty of Wad-Ras enlarged Ceuta's territory
sources.source: Treaty of Wad-Ras, 26 April 1860; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hispano-Moroccan War'

sources.claim: In 1912 France and Spain divided Morocco into protectorates, Spain taking a northern strip
sources.source: Treaty of Fez, 30 March 1912, and Franco-Spanish Convention, 27 November 1912

sources.claim: Morocco became independent in 1956; Spain returned its northern zone but kept Ceuta and Melilla
sources.source: Spanish-Moroccan Joint Declaration, 7 April 1956; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Morocco'

sources.claim: Spain's position is that Ceuta and Melilla were never part of the protectorate
sources.source: Peter Gold, 'Europe or Africa?', 2000

sources.claim: Spain joined the European Community on 1 January 1986
sources.source: Treaty of Accession of Spain and Portugal, in force 1 January 1986

sources.claim: Ceuta began fencing its border in 1993 and Melilla in 1998, partly with EU funds
sources.source: Peter Gold, 'Europe or Africa?', 2000; Human Rights Watch, 'Spain: The Other Face of the Canary Islands' and related reports

sources.claim: Morocco calls the cities Sebta and Mlilya and has never recognised Spanish sovereignty
sources.source: Peter Gold, 'Europe or Africa?', 2000; Moroccan official usage

sources.claim: Morocco argues the cities are colonial leftovers that its territorial integrity should end, and points to the return of Hong Kong and Macau
sources.source: Peter Gold, 'Europe or Africa?', 2000

sources.claim: Hong Kong returned to China in 1997 and Macau in 1999
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hong Kong' and 'Macau'

sources.claim: Supporters of Morocco's claim compare it with Spain's claim to Gibraltar
sources.source: Peter Gold, 'Europe or Africa?', 2000

sources.claim: In December 2020 Morocco's then prime minister called Ceuta and Melilla Moroccan, and Spain summoned Morocco's ambassador
sources.source: Reuters and El País, 21 December 2020

sources.claim: Ceuta and Melilla are not on the UN list of non-self-governing territories; Gibraltar is
sources.source: United Nations, Special Committee on Decolonization, list of Non-Self-Governing Territories

sources.claim: Each city has been an autonomous city since 1995 and elects one deputy to Spain's Congress
sources.source: Organic Laws 1/1995 and 2/1995, 13 March 1995; Spanish electoral law (LOREG)

sources.claim: Goods reached the cities at low tax and were carried into Morocco by porters, many of them women
sources.source: Spanish Ombudsman (Defensor del Pueblo) reports on porters, 2016-2019; El País reporting

sources.claim: Morocco closed the commercial customs post at Melilla in August 2018
sources.source: El País, August 2018

sources.claim: Morocco stopped the porter trade at Ceuta in October 2019, citing harm to its economy
sources.source: Reuters, October 2019

sources.claim: Both land borders closed in March 2020, amid the pandemic, and reopened on 17 May 2022, over two years later
sources.source: Spanish Ministry of the Interior, March 2020 and 17 May 2022

sources.claim: About 10,000 people entered Ceuta in two days in May 2021, by Spanish government figures
sources.source: Spanish government figures, 17-18 May 2021, reported by Reuters and BBC

sources.claim: Weeks earlier Spain had admitted Polisario leader Brahim Ghali to a hospital in Logroño
sources.source: Reuters, April-May 2021

sources.claim: Spain said Morocco used the border as pressure; Morocco said Spain had broken trust
sources.source: Statements by Spain's government and Morocco's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, May 2021, reported by Reuters

sources.claim: Western Sahara is disputed: Morocco controls most of it and the Polisario Front seeks independence
sources.source: United Nations, MINURSO mandate; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Western Sahara'

sources.claim: In March 2022 Spain called Morocco's autonomy plan 'the most serious, realistic and credible basis' for resolving the dispute
sources.source: Letter from Spain's Prime Minister to King Mohammed VI, March 2022, as published by Morocco's Royal Cabinet and confirmed by Spain's government, 18 March 2022

sources.claim: In June 2022 migrants died at Melilla's border: 23 by Moroccan authorities' count, at least 37 according to Amnesty International
sources.source: Moroccan authorities, June 2022; Amnesty International, December 2022

sources.claim: Moroccan authorities blamed a crush at the fence; Amnesty International blamed violent force by security forces
sources.source: Moroccan Interior Ministry statements, June 2022, reported by Reuters; Amnesty International report on Melilla, December 2022

sources.claim: In January 2025 the first trucks of goods crossed under a new customs arrangement
sources.source: El País and Reuters, January 2025

sources.claim: EU-Morocco trade in goods was about 60 billion euros in 2023
sources.source: European Commission, DG Trade, EU-Morocco trade relations page, 2024

sources.claim: Morocco built Tanger Med, about 20 km west of Ceuta, which opened in 2007
sources.source: Tanger Med Port Authority (TMSA); distance measured on map

sources.claim: In 2023 Tanger Med handled about 8.6 million TEU, more than Valencia (about 4.8 million) or Algeciras (about 4.7 million)
sources.source: Tanger Med 2023 activity report; Valenciaport 2023 statistics; Port of Algeciras (APBA) 2023 statistics

sources.claim: NATO Article 6 covers attacks on the territory of the Parties in Europe or North America
sources.source: North Atlantic Treaty, Article 6, 1949 (as amended 1951)

sources.claim: Experts disagree on whether NATO's mutual defence covers Ceuta and Melilla
sources.source: Elcano Royal Institute analysis, 2022; Peter Gold, 'Europe or Africa?', 2000

sources.claim: Moroccan soldiers landed on Perejil on 11 July 2002; Spanish troops removed them on 17 July; US mediation left the islet empty
sources.source: BBC News and The Guardian, July 2002

sources.claim: Gibraltar lies about 28 km north of Ceuta
sources.source: Distance measured on map

sources.claim: In June 2025 the EU and the UK agreed on removing checks at Gibraltar's land border
sources.source: Joint statement of the European Commission, UK and Spain, 11 June 2025

sources.claim: Llívia is a Spanish town surrounded by France, kept because the 1659 treaty ceded villages and Llívia counted as a town
sources.source: Treaty of the Pyrenees, 1659, and the Treaty of Llívia, 1660; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Llívia'
